source.title: Non-Gaussianity Reveals Interpretable Directions in Language Models
source.authors: Si-Da Liu; Fei-Jiang Han; Sarah Wiegreffe; Fu-Rong Huang

page_placements.theme: Dense structure, anisotropy and privileged representation bases

record.tranche_reason: The study reports results on interpretable directions and SAE features in LLM activations, extending the feature-geometry discussion to language models rather than testing the original toy-network setup.
record.gate_note: The paper also reports reconstruction, probing, targeted perturbation, and generation-steering results. Those evaluate the utility of its coordinates or interventions, rather than directly testing the claim versions here, so they are not rows. Results cited from prior work are excluded.
record.test_reason: The paper measures LLM residual-stream activations directly. It shows that projections onto public SAE decoder directions are far more heavy-tailed than random or PCA projections, which bears on V4's sparse, SAE-recoverable structure. It also measures how far a complete ICA basis is covered by SAE dictionaries, which bears weakly on V5's completeness. Most other results evaluate the authors' ICA method.
record.authors_conclusion: Broadly right. The authors also stress three points. A sign-sensitive evaluation bias made earlier work underestimate ICA, and skewness-based tail selection recovers much of the gap to SAEs. Excess kurtosis correlates with auto-interp (ρs=0.45) and with human confidence. ICA coordinates are competitive with SAEs on reconstruction, probing and TPP while being much cheaper. They position ICA as a compact first lens, not an SAE replacement.
record.recipe_differences: The study uses centered and whitened LLM residual-stream activations and symmetric FastICA to find non-Gaussian directions. It does not use the original toy-network feature-generation and sparsity sweep.
record.method_sensitivity: Interpretability evaluation depends on ICA sign orientation: choosing the skewness-selected tail substantially changes scores. Fitting budget, training corpus, and evaluator also affect absolute evaluation scores, though the authors report the sign-correction pattern persists across these checks.

fits_no_version.finding: A complete (d-component, non-overcomplete) ICA basis, once its sign is corrected by skewness, reaches auto-interp scores competitive with overcomplete public SAEs. Arbitrary-sign evaluation reproduces the earlier reported gap.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Interpretable directions comparable to SAE features can be recovered without an overcomplete sparse dictionary; earlier ICA-SAE gaps reflected a sign-evaluation artifact.

fits_no_version.finding: About 80–84% of randomly sampled ICA components receive high-confidence human labels in three LLMs.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: ICA recovers interpretable directions in LLM residual streams.

fits_no_version.finding: In Qwen3-32B layer-0 MLP neurons, excess kurtosis correlates with lexical concentration (ρs=0.55). All sampled neurons have kurtosis ≥11.34, versus ~0 for random residual directions.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Native neuron (privileged-basis) activations are strongly non-Gaussian, and kurtosis tracks lexical selectivity.

record.problems: The main excess-kurtosis and overlap plots do not provide exact values in the text. The overlap measure is a geometric cosine comparison and does not by itself establish representation completeness. Tokenwise response comparisons are illustrative single-sentence visualizations, and SAE feature stability or canonicality is not tested.
record.rows_left_out: No additional claim-relevant results were left out. Other downstream reconstruction, sparse-probing, targeted-perturbation, and generation-intervention results were excluded because they evaluate the utility of the study's coordinates or induced interventions rather than the claim versions.

untested.parts: No toy models, no sparsity sweep, no phase transition, no geometry of superposed features.
No test of capacity competition or feature importance as the cause of polysemanticity.
No test of polysemantic neurons arising without capacity pressure. The 'bank' polysemy decomposition concerns words, not neurons.
Does not test whether features are spread across many neurons. The MLP-neuron analysis (r16) measures kurtosis and lexical concentration, not distributedness.
SAE feature stability across runs, and whether SAE features are canonical units. Seed stability is measured for ICA only.
Does not test one- versus multi-dimensional features.

record.verdict_notes: Removed the V4 links on r4–r6: these compare the study's own method with SAEs and do not test whether LLMs contain SAE-recoverable sparse features. They also do not challenge V4, and are recorded under fits_no_version. Unlinked r10–r12 (illustrative single sentence). The V5 limits_scope verdict is weak: incomplete ICA–SAE overlap suggests the SAE dictionaries miss some non-Gaussian structure, but the paper does not show the missed directions are meaningful features. ICA is capped at d components, so it cannot test superposition beyond d directions. All key V4/V5 values are in figures only.

versions.untested_parts: No toy-network feature-count or sparsity sweep, superposition transition, or regular geometry test.
No test of capacity competition, feature importance, or dedicated versus shared dimensions as an explanation of polysemanticity.
The paper discusses contextual mixtures and polysemy, but does not test whether polysemantic neurons arise without capacity pressure.
The paper tests interpretability and non-Gaussian structure of SAE decoder directions and compares ICA directions with SAE features. It does not test whether features are spread across many neurons.
It measures ICA-to-SAE directional overlap and compares tokenwise responses, but does not test SAE feature stability across training runs or establish whether SAE features are canonical units.
The paper studies individual ICA directions but does not test whether the underlying represented features are one-dimensional rather than multidimensional.

rows.subject: Pythia 70M
rows.operation_detail: Reproduced the released ICA–SAE explanation-prediction interpretability comparison using the arbitrary positive ICA tail.
rows.measure: Automated interpretability score, Pearson correlation between predicted and observed token-level scores
rows.baseline: Public SAE baseline; exact plotted values figure only.
rows.value: The previously reported gap between SAE and arbitrary-sign ICA is reproduced.
rows.uncertainty: 95% intervals shown in Figure 4; numerical values not stated
rows.note: This is the uncorrected-sign comparison; the paper says it recovers the previously reported gap.
rows.check: Compares the study's own method (arbitrary-sign ICA) with SAE auto-interp scores. It does not measure whether models contain SAE-recoverable sparse features, and 'partial' has no meaning against V4.

rows.subject: Pythia 70M
rows.operation_detail: Re-evaluated the same fitted ICA directions using the skewness-selected stronger tail.
rows.measure: Automated interpretability score, Pearson correlation between predicted and observed token-level scores
rows.baseline: Public SAE baseline; exact plotted values figure only.
rows.value: Much of the gap disappears and ICA becomes competitive with SAE.
rows.uncertainty: 95% intervals shown in Figure 4; numerical values not stated
rows.note: The fitted ICA directions are unchanged; the evaluation tail is changed.
rows.check: Compares the study's method with SAE (sign-corrected ICA competitive with SAE), not a test of V4. Belongs under fits_no_version.

rows.subject: Qwen 3.5 9B Base
rows.operation_detail: Compared skewness-oriented ICA components with the public SAE using explanation-prediction evaluation.

conditions.value: thinkingmachines/Inkling for explanations; Qwen3.8-27B for prediction

rows.measure: Automated interpretability score, Pearson correlation between predicted and observed token-level scores
rows.baseline: Public SAE baseline; exact plotted values figure only.
rows.value: Sign-corrected ICA is competitive with the public SAE.
rows.uncertainty: 95% intervals shown in Figure 4; numerical values not stated
rows.note: Figure 4 plots means over 150 components with 95% intervals.
rows.check: Same as r5: a comparison of ICA with SAE on Qwen 3.5 9B Base, not a measure of V4.

rows.subject: GPT-2 Small
rows.operation_detail: Compared each ICA residual-space writing direction with its nearest same-layer SAE decoder direction by absolute cosine.

conditions.value: ICA directions versus matched SAE dictionary

rows.measure: Maximum absolute cosine to any SAE decoder direction
rows.baseline: Matched isotropic random directions; exact values figure only.
rows.value: ICA overlap is shifted above the random reference, but the distribution is broad and includes directions with weaker SAE alignment.
rows.uncertainty: Median and interquartile ranges shown by layer; exact values figure only
rows.note: The paper characterizes ICA and SAE as recovering overlapping but complementary structure.
rows.check: Bears on SAE completeness only indirectly. The weakly aligned ICA directions are not shown to be interpretable features missing from the SAE, so incompleteness is suggested rather than established. Values are in figures only.

source_check.correct: state=cannot_determine for V5; versions=none. Nearest-SAE alignment exceeds the random reference but varies broadly. The analysis does not establish that weakly aligned directions are interpretable features missing from the dictionary.
source_check.problem: Incomplete directional overlap does not establish incomplete, unstable or noncanonical SAE feature units.

rows.subject: Qwen3-32B
rows.operation_detail: Measured excess kurtosis and lexical concentration in a random sample of native MLP neurons.

conditions.value: 10,000 Pile-10k documents; 15,392,600 token positions per neuron

rows.measure: Spearman association of excess kurtosis with lexical concentration; mean concentration by kurtosis quartile
rows.value: Spearman ρs = 0.55; highest kurtosis quartile mean concentration: 80.8%.
rows.uncertainty: A second concentration calculation using one extreme position per document gives ρs = 0.53.
rows.note: The authors describe this as preliminary evidence that kurtosis may help prioritize neurons with concentrated lexical responses.

relationships.condition: Public SAE decoder directions, all evaluated layers of GPT-2 Small, Gemma 2 2B and Qwen 3.5 9B Base, 1M held-out activations per layer
relationships.reason: Projections onto SAE decoder directions are far more heavy-tailed than random projections (near-Gaussian) and than PCA, consistent with sparse SAE-recoverable structure (r1–r3). Values are in Figure 3 only.
relationships.display_finding: Activations projected onto SAE decoder directions were far more heavy-tailed than random projections, which were near-Gaussian, and than PCA, consistent with sparse structure an SAE can recover.

relationships.condition: ICA writing directions vs same-layer public SAE dictionaries, GPT-2 Small, Gemma 2 2B and Qwen 3.5 9B Base
